summary: Specifies the Initial Connection Protocol, the third-level procedure for connecting a user process, typically Telnet, to a server process, typically a logger, at another site. It describes a family of such protocols and the values for connecting Telnets to loggers. It replaced RFC 123, RFC 143 and RFC 145.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC describes how one program first connects to a service on another host. The initial connection returns socket numbers that the two hosts use to establish the service connections.

subtitle: A procedure for opening connections between a user process and a server process on different hosts.

tldr.problem: A user process at one site needed a defined way to connect to a server process at another site.
tldr.mechanism: The user contacts a known server socket, receives a new socket number, then establishes the service connections using the assigned sockets.
tldr.outcome: The document describes a family of Initial Connection Protocols and specific Telnet-to-Logger parameters. It obsoletes RFCs 123, 143 and 145.

today: RFC 165 is listed as Unknown and obsoletes RFC 123, RFC 143 and RFC 145.

sections.title: What the Initial Connection Protocol Does
sections.content:
The Initial Connection Protocol (ICP) connects a user process at one site with a server process at another. Telnet connecting to a Logger is one example, but the RFC says other combinations are possible.

The document describes the procedure at the user-process level and at the Network Control Program (NCP) level. It defines operations such as Init, Listen, Send, Receive and Close.
sections.plainLanguage: An ICP is the setup exchange between a program requesting a service and the program providing it. The RFC explains the exchange both as program operations and as NCP commands.

sections.title: The User-Level Connection Sequence
sections.content:
The server listens on a well-advertised send socket L. The user connects from receive socket U, using a byte size of 32. The server sends a 32-bit even number S and closes the initial connection. The server then uses sockets S and S+1, which connect to user sockets U+3 and U+2.

The RFC requires L to be a send socket, the byte sizes to be legal, and each L to have only one associated pair of byte sizes. These restrictions keep separate services from sharing the same server socket and being distinguished only by byte size.
sections.plainLanguage: The server listens on a known socket and returns a new socket number to the user. Both hosts then use the new socket numbers for the service connections.

sections.title: NCP Commands and Telnet Parameters
sections.content:
At the NCP level, the exchange uses RTS, STR, ALL and CLS control commands. The user requests a connection, the hosts allocate capacity to send the socket number, and they close the initial connection before establishing the service sockets. Some setup steps may occur in parallel.

The RFC specifies a message allocation of 1, a bit allocation of 32 and a byte size of 32 for the initial socket number. For a Telnet-to-Logger connection, L is 1 and the server byte size is 8. The RFC notes that some hosts may send the 32-bit socket number as four 8-bit bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: The NCP commands perform the same setup using network control messages. The RFC gives specific values for the initial connection and for Telnet connecting to a Logger.

messages.label: Send S, then close L

messages.note: Server sockets S and S+1 connect to user sockets U+3 and U+2.
